_why: Capability OBSERVATIONS about the three harnesses, each pinned to the version it was measured on. Codex and Antigravity ship almost daily, so a sentence like 'this flag does not exist' is evidence about one build, never a ruling. npm run harness:usage compares measuredOn with the installed version and prints every observation that is now UNVERIFIED, with the probe that re-settles it. A CONSTRAINT is different: it comes from our own rules or a contract we own, does not lapse with a release, and is listed here only so a reader can tell the two apart. Append; never delete - a lapsed observation gets re-measured and its measuredOn moves.

observations.claim: claude-sonnet-4-6 and claude-opus-4-6-thinking reject --effort outright (status ERROR, 0 s, 0 tokens); the Gemini and GPT-OSS ids carry their tier in the model name.
observations.reprobe: Any --effort call on those ids: scripts/agy-run.mjs downgrades its refusal to a warning on a version other than measuredOn, so the next such call IS the probe. Update EFFORTLESS_MODELS there and measuredOn here with the result.

observations.claim: agy keeps no cumulative usage on disk and has no usage or quota subcommand; per-run usage exists once on stdout, which is why scripts/agy-run.mjs is the only record of Antigravity spend.
observations.reprobe: agy --help for a usage/quota subcommand, and a text scan of ~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/ for a token field after one run.
observations.source: scripts/agy-run.mjs header; docs/HARNESS_ROUTING.md "Cost, and what a usage meter can read"

observations.claim: Fourteen models in two pools: eleven Gemini ids (3.8/3.7/3.6 flash at three tiers, 3.1 pro at two) on the Gemini meter; claude-sonnet-4-6, claude-opus-4-6-thinking and gpt-oss-120b-medium on the second meter. gemini-3.7-flash-high remains the measured default for comprehension (3.8 tied on correctness and was 5.3x slower).
observations.reprobe: agy models; then the 3.8-vs-3.7 recheck in docs/HARNESS_ROUTING.md if the list changed.

observations.claim: codex agents is a TUI with no --json or list-and-exit mode, so Codex jobs cannot join the third liveness signal the way claude agents --json does; codex queue is fire-and-forget into a thread you already hold.
observations.source: docs/HARNESS_ROUTING.md, "The two unmeasured Codex surfaces, probed 2026-09-03"

observations.claim: Codex writes a rate_limits snapshot into its rollout only when one of its own sessions runs, so the capacity reading can be absent or stale; availability is three-valued (headroom / low / UNKNOWN) and is never probed with a paid call.
observations.reprobe: npm run harness:usage after a Codex session; the snapshot line names its own timestamp.
observations.source: docs/HARNESS_ROUTING.md, "Owner ruling 2026-09-01: route by pool capacity"

observations.claim: An Agent call with isolation: "remote" is ACCEPTED and runs on this laptop anyway, in an ordinary local worktree (hostname Legion-001, win32, .claude/worktrees/agent-<id>). The launch reports success and nothing says the isolation was dropped, so a wave routing rows to "cloud" spends the local RAM it meant to save while the plan still reads as honoured.
observations.reprobe: Launch any agent with isolation: "remote" whose first step is `node scripts/agent-isolation.mjs --expect remote`. Exit 1 with ISOLATION MISMATCH confirms it; exit 0 refutes it and this entry moves.

observations.claim: scripts/agy-run.mjs refuses --dangerously-skip-permissions rather than forwarding it, and a write runs only in a linked worktree on a feature branch. This is our rule, not a fact about agy, and it does not lapse with a release.

A Codex row always names a fallback pool, because Codex capacity is shared with the owner's other projects and can be near zero on a given day. Codex is otherwise available by default (owner, 2026-09-03) - this constrains the plan's shape, not how much Codex it uses.
